title: Error-Handling Strategy at Scale
summary: In Go, `error` is just an interface `{ Error() string }` — but turning that into a coherent strategy across a large system is a craft. The discipline is: **wrap with context at each layer** (`%w`), **classify** errors (retryable vs terminal, user vs internal), **inspect** them with `errors.Is`/`errors.As`, and **map** them to transport codes at the boundary — all while handling each error exactly once.

subtopics.title: error is just an interface
subtopics.explanation: error is the one-method interface `interface { Error() string }`. Any type with an Error() string method is an error. Idiomatically it's the last return value, and the caller checks `if err != nil` before trusting the other results. Because it's an ordinary interface, an error-handling strategy is built entirely from plain Go values — no exceptions, no magic.

subtopics.title: Sentinel errors
subtopics.explanation: A sentinel is a package-level error value (`var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")`) representing a known condition. Callers compare against it with errors.Is — never with ==, because wrapping breaks ==. Define sentinels in the package that owns the domain. Sentinels are the stable, wrap-safe vocabulary your layers use to communicate known failure conditions across a large system.

subtopics.title: Wrapping with %w
subtopics.explanation: fmt.Errorf("loading user %d: %w", id, err) adds human context AND preserves the wrapped error in a chain. %w keeps the chain (so errors.Is/As can walk it); %v formats the error into a string and DROPS the chain. Wrap to add value, not noise. Wrapping with %w at each layer is how context accumulates up the stack while the original cause stays inspectable — the backbone of the strategy.

subtopics.title: Inspecting the chain: Is vs As
subtopics.explanation: errors.Is(err, target) walks the chain looking for a matching sentinel (value equality or a custom Is). errors.As(err, &target) walks the chain looking for an error assignable to target's type, and on success populates it so you can read its fields/codes. Choosing Is for identity and As for typed extraction is exactly how the boundary inspects a wrapped error to decide the response.

subtopics.title: Custom error types
subtopics.explanation: Define a struct with an Error() method to carry structured data (codes, resource names, retryability). Add an Unwrap() method so it participates in the chain and errors.Is/As can see through it. Query it with errors.As. Custom types let your strategy carry machine-readable classification (status codes, retryability) alongside the human message.

subtopics.title: Classify and map at the boundary
subtopics.explanation: Internally, classify errors (retryable, terminal, validation, not-found). At the transport edge — HTTP handler, gRPC server — map domain errors to status codes and a safe client message, log once with structured fields, and never leak internal details (stack traces, SQL) to the client. This handle-once mapping at exactly one boundary is what keeps logs clean and clients safe across the whole system.

subtopics.title: Combining failures with errors.Join
subtopics.explanation: errors.Join (Go 1.20+) combines several errors into one whose Unwrap returns a []error, and errors.Is/As check every joined error. It's ideal for accumulating validation failures or the errors from fanned-out work. Join is the strategy's tool for reporting multiple simultaneous failures without losing any of them to the chain-walkers.

foundations.overview: Go has no exceptions for ordinary failures — it returns errors as values. That sounds primitive, but it forces a deliberate decision at every call site: handle it, wrap it with context and return it, or ignore it. At scale, across dozens of packages and service boundaries, ad-hoc error handling becomes a liability: errors lose their origin, callers can't tell retryable failures from terminal ones, and internal details leak to clients. A strategy fixes this by treating errors as first-class, structured data that flows from the deepest layer up to the boundary, accumulating context but staying inspectable.
foundations.formalDefinition: An error in Go is any value implementing the built-in interface `error { Error() string }`. The standard library defines a wrapping protocol: an error may implement `Unwrap() error` (or `Unwrap() []error`) to expose a cause chain, and `errors.Is`, `errors.As`, and `errors.Unwrap` traverse that chain to test identity, extract concrete types, and peel one layer respectively.
foundations.whyItMatters: Errors are how a system communicates failure, and failure is where production systems live or die. A coherent strategy means an on-call engineer can read one log line and know what failed, where, and whether it's retryable — while the client gets a clean, safe message and the right status code. It's also one of the highest-signal topics in senior Go interviews because it reveals whether you think about systems, not just syntax.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture an error as a package being shipped up through the layers of your application. Each layer that handles it can slap a new label on the box ('failed while loading user', 'failed during checkout') with `%w`, but the original contents stay sealed inside. At the loading dock (the transport boundary) someone opens the box, reads the labels with errors.Is/As to decide where it goes (404? retry? alert?), logs the full manifest once, and hands the customer only a clean summary.
foundations.runtimePerspective: Wrapping is cheap: fmt.Errorf with %w allocates a small *wrapError struct holding the message and the wrapped error pointer — a linked list, not a copy of anything heavy. errors.Is/As walk that list with a loop, calling Unwrap until they hit nil; cost is proportional to chain depth (usually tiny). There is no stack unwinding, no exception machinery — an error is an ordinary heap value, and `if err != nil` is an ordinary branch the compiler can predict well.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Repository layers return wrapped sentinels (ErrNotFound) to services; services classify and add business context; HTTP/gRPC handlers map domain errors to 404/409/500 and emit structured logs and metrics; clients of remote APIs wrap transport errors as retryable so a retry layer can act on them.
foundations.businessImpact: Good error classification directly affects revenue and trust: correctly distinguishing a transient downstream blip (retry, succeed) from a real failure (fail fast, alert) reduces both lost transactions and false-alarm pages. Clean client-facing errors reduce support tickets; leak-free errors reduce security incidents.
foundations.engineeringImpact: A shared error strategy lets teams compose packages without coordination: a caller can rely on errors.Is(err, repo.ErrNotFound) regardless of how deep the failure originated. It shrinks debugging time because every error carries its trail, and it kills whole bug classes (swallowed errors, double-logging, == comparisons that silently break on wrapping).
foundations.performanceImpact: Error handling is on the cold path by design, so wrapping cost is negligible. The real performance trap is logging: logging the same error at every layer (double/triple logging) floods log pipelines and storage. Handle-once — log at the boundary, return everywhere else — keeps log volume and cost bounded.
commonUseCases: Wrapping repository errors with %w and exposing sentinels
Classifying retryable vs terminal errors for a retry layer
Mapping domain errors to HTTP/gRPC status at the boundary
Extracting structured fields (codes, resource IDs) with errors.As

commonMisconceptions.myth: You should compare errors with == against a known value.
commonMisconceptions.reality: == breaks the moment the error is wrapped. Use errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound), which walks the whole chain. Reserve == for the rare unwrapped-by-contract case.
%w wraps and preserves the chain so errors.Is/As can see the cause; %v formats it into a string and discards the chain. Use %w when you want the cause to remain inspectable.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You should log an error and also return it.
commonMisconceptions.reality: That double-logs as the error climbs the stack. Handle once: either log it (you're the boundary) or return/wrap it (someone above will handle it) — not both.

commonMisconceptions.myth: panic/recover is Go's exception mechanism for errors.
commonMisconceptions.reality: panic is for truly unrecoverable, programmer-level faults (impossible states). Ordinary, expected failures are returned as error values; using panic for control flow is an anti-pattern.

visualExplorer.title: error is a one-method interface
visualExplorer.caption: Any type with an Error() string method satisfies error. Wrapping types add an Unwrap() error method so errors.Is/As can traverse the cause chain.

visualExplorer.caption: How context is added going up the stack with %w, then inspected at the boundary with errors.Is/As.

config.intro: Follow one failure from the database driver up to the HTTP response:

steps.name: Origin (driver)
steps.detail: The SQL driver returns sql.ErrNoRows. The repository translates it into a domain sentinel: `return fmt.Errorf("user %d: %w", id, ErrNotFound)`.

steps.name: Wrap with context (service)
steps.detail: The service adds business context but keeps the chain: `return fmt.Errorf("checkout for user %d: %w", id, err)`. The chain is now checkout -> user -> ErrNotFound.

steps.name: Arrive at the boundary (handler)
steps.detail: The HTTP handler receives the fully-wrapped error. This is the single place that decides the outcome — it handles the error exactly once.

steps.name: Inspect with Is / As
steps.detail: `errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound)` walks the chain and matches the sentinel; `errors.As(err, &validationErr)` would extract a typed error to read its fields.

steps.name: Map & log once
steps.detail: Map to HTTP 404, write a clean client message ('user not found'), and log the full wrapped chain ONCE with structured fields. Internal details never reach the client.

interactiveExamples.title: Wrap a sentinel, then walk the chain with errors.Is
interactiveExamples.explanation: The repository wraps a package sentinel with %w. The service wraps again, still with %w, preserving the chain. At the top, errors.Is finds ErrNotFound no matter how deep it is — while == would have failed.

code.expectedOutput:
checkout: repo: user 42: not found
is ErrNotFound: true
== ErrNotFound: false

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: extract a typed error with errors.As
interactiveExamples.explanation: A sentinel tells you WHAT failed; a custom error type tells you the details. Use errors.As to pull the *NotFoundError out of the chain and read its fields. Fill in the As call so the program prints the missing resource and id.

checkpoints.code:
var ErrClosed = errors.New("closed")
wrapped := fmt.Errorf("write failed: %w", ErrClosed)
fmt.Println(errors.Is(wrapped, ErrClosed))
fmt.Println(errors.Unwrap(wrapped) == ErrClosed)
checkpoints.explanation: %w wraps ErrClosed, so errors.Is finds it by walking the chain (true). errors.Unwrap peels exactly one layer, returning the directly-wrapped ErrClosed, so == is also true here. (== would fail only if there were extra layers between them.)

checkpoints.prompt: You want the cause to remain inspectable by errors.Is/As after formatting. Which is correct?
options: Use %v — it preserves the wrapped error
Use %w — it wraps and preserves the chain
checkpoints.explanation: Only %w wraps: it stores the underlying error so errors.Is/As can traverse it. %v, %s, and %+v format the error into a plain string and discard the chain, making later inspection impossible.

checkpoints.prompt: A repository miss should be detectable as ErrNotFound at the top, but errors.Is always returns false. Why?
options: The format verb is %v, which flattens ErrNotFound to text and drops the chain
ErrNotFound must be a struct, not errors.New
checkpoints.explanation: %v formats ErrNotFound into the message string but does NOT wrap it, so there is no chain for errors.Is to walk. Changing the verb to %w preserves the sentinel and makes errors.Is return true.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the boundary check so a not-found anywhere in the chain maps to HTTP 404.
checkpoints.codeBefore:
func handle(w http.ResponseWriter, err error) {
    if
checkpoints.explanation: errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) walks the whole wrapped chain, so it matches even when the sentinel is buried under context. == fails on wrapping, errors.As needs a pointer-to-type (not a sentinel value), and comparing Error() strings is brittle.

codeLab.title: Classify errors with a sentinel and a typed error
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Classify(err error) string`. Return "not_found" if the chain contains the sentinel ErrNotFound (use errors.Is). Return "validation" if the chain contains a *ValidationError (use errors.As). Return "none" for a nil error, and "unknown" for anything else. Both helper types are provided.
hints: Check err == nil first and return "none".
Use errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) for the sentinel — it walks the chain so wrapping doesn't matter.
Declare `var ve *ValidationError` and use errors.As(err, &ve) to extract the typed error from the chain.

debuggingLab.title: errors.Is can't find the sentinel after wrapping
debuggingLab.symptom: The repository returns a wrapped error, but the handler's errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) is always false, so every miss becomes a 500 instead of a 404.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The bug is the format verb. %v renders ErrNotFound into the message string but creates no link to the underlying error, so the returned error has an empty cause chain. errors.Is walks the chain via Unwrap and finds nothing matching ErrNotFound, so it returns false and the handler falls through to 500.
commonMistakes: Using %v (or %s) instead of %w when you intend the cause to stay inspectable.
Assuming errors.Is matches on the error's text rather than on chain identity.
Comparing with == against a sentinel that has been wrapped.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Change the format verb so the sentinel is wrapped and the chain is preserved, making errors.Is return true.

theory.question: What is the difference between errors.Is and errors.As, and when do you use each?
theory.directAnswer: errors.Is(err, target) reports whether target appears anywhere in err's wrapped chain — you use it to test for a known sentinel value like ErrNotFound. errors.As(err, &target) finds the first error in the chain assignable to target's type and assigns it, so you can read that concrete type's fields — you use it to extract a custom error type like *ValidationError. Rule of thumb: Is for identity (which known error), As for type (give me the typed error so I can read its data).

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two chain-walking helpers from the errors package: Is tests value/identity equality, As tests and extracts by concrete type.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Once errors are wrapped with %w, == and type assertions no longer work directly because the value/type you want is buried under layers. Is/As traverse the chain for you.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Both call Unwrap repeatedly. Is compares each link to target (and respects a custom Is method if present). As checks if each link is assignable to *target's element type and, on a match, assigns it and returns true.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing the wrong one (or using == / type assertions) is a classic source of bugs where wrapped errors silently stop matching.
theory.realWorldExample: A handler calls errors.Is(err, repo.ErrNotFound) to return 404, and errors.As(err, &ve) to pull a *ValidationError's field name into a 400 response body.

followUps.question: What must the second argument to errors.As be?
followUps.answer: A non-nil pointer to either a type implementing error or to an interface; otherwise As panics. Typically `var ve *MyError; errors.As(err, &ve)`.

followUps.question: Can a type customize errors.Is behavior?
followUps.answer: Yes — implement `Is(target error) bool` on the type, and errors.Is will call it instead of value comparison, useful for matching a family of errors.

theory.question: Explain the difference between %w and %v in fmt.Errorf, and the 'handle once' principle.
theory.directAnswer: %w wraps the error: fmt.Errorf stores the underlying error so the returned error has an Unwrap method and errors.Is/As can traverse it. %v formats the error into the message string and discards the link — the chain ends there. The 'handle once' principle says each error should be acted on exactly once: lower layers wrap-and-return (adding context), and exactly one layer — usually the transport boundary — logs it and decides the outcome. Logging at every layer double-logs and floods your logs.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: %w is the wrapping verb; %v is a formatting verb. 'Handle once' is the discipline of choosing a single place to terminate an error.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Wrapping lets context accumulate while keeping the cause inspectable; handle-once prevents both lost context and noisy duplicate logging.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: %w builds a linked list of errors; the boundary walks it with Is/As, logs the full chain once with structured fields, maps it to a transport code, and returns a sanitized message to the client.

theory.whyImportant: It's the core of a scalable strategy: it keeps errors debuggable end-to-end while keeping log volume and client-facing leakage under control.
theory.realWorldExample: A repo returns `fmt.Errorf("query: %w", err)`; the service returns `fmt.Errorf("checkout: %w", err)`; only the HTTP handler logs the chain and writes a 500 with a generic message.

followUps.question: When should you NOT wrap?
followUps.answer: When wrapping adds no value (no new context) or when you deliberately want to hide the underlying cause from callers — then format with %v to drop the chain, or return a fresh sentinel.

followUps.question: What does errors.Join do?
followUps.answer: Go 1.20's errors.Join(errs...) combines multiple errors into one whose Unwrap returns []error; errors.Is/As check all of them. Useful for accumulating validation failures or multi-step cleanup errors.

theory.question: Compare sentinel errors, typed errors, and opaque errors as error contracts across an API boundary. Which do you expose, and what does each commit you to maintaining?
theory.directAnswer: These are three levels of coupling you offer callers. A *sentinel* (`var ErrNotFound = errors.New(...)`) is a shared identity value callers match with errors.Is — cheap and precise, but it becomes part of your public API forever and any package importing it now depends on you. A *typed* error (a struct with Error() and fields, matched with errors.As) is richer: callers can read structured data (a failing field, a status code, retryability), but you've committed to the struct's exported fields and its type identity as API. An *opaque* error is one you return with no promise about identity or type — callers can only display it or check nothing beyond `!= nil`; this gives you maximum freedom to change internals but tells callers nothing programmatic. The rule: expose sentinels/typed errors ONLY for conditions callers must branch on (not-found, conflict, validation), keep everything else opaque, and always wrap with %w internally so the chain stays inspectable even when the public contract is opaque.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Three strategies for what an error communicates to a caller: identity (sentinel), type+data (typed), or nothing programmatic (opaque).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Every error you let callers match becomes a maintenance obligation; distinguishing what's a public contract from what's an internal detail keeps your API evolvable while still letting callers handle the cases they genuinely need to branch on.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Sentinels are matched by errors.Is (value identity, possibly via a custom Is method); typed errors are extracted by errors.As (assignability to a concrete/interface type) so fields can be read; opaque errors expose neither, so callers can only wrap, log, or display them.

theory.whyImportant: Over-exposing errors (turning every internal failure into a public sentinel) freezes your implementation; under-exposing them forces callers into brittle string matching. Getting the contract right is central to a scalable strategy.
theory.realWorldExample: database/sql exposes sql.ErrNoRows as a sentinel because callers must branch on it, while most driver-internal failures are effectively opaque; a repository translates ErrNoRows into its own domain sentinel with %w so its callers don't couple to the driver.

followUps.question: How do you make an error opaque yet still classifiable internally?
followUps.answer: Return it opaque to external callers (no exported sentinel/type) but internally wrap the real cause with %w and, if needed, tag it with an unexported marker type queried via errors.As inside your own package — external callers see only `!= nil`, your own boundary can still classify it.

followUps.question: Why prefer errors.Is over exporting a comparable sentinel that callers use with ==?
followUps.answer: == breaks the instant the sentinel is wrapped with %w anywhere in the chain; errors.Is walks the whole chain, so exposing 'match with errors.Is' as the contract lets you add wrapping context freely without breaking callers.

theory.question: Give a decision rule for whether to handle, annotate (wrap with %w), or flatten (%v) / replace an error at a given call site. What goes wrong at each layer if you choose badly?
theory.directAnswer: At each call site you have four choices and a rule for each. HANDLE it (log/recover/return a default) only if this is the layer that can actually resolve it or the designated boundary — handling too early hides failures from callers who needed to know. ANNOTATE with %w when you're passing it upward and can add context that aids debugging ('checkout for user 42: %w') AND callers legitimately need to inspect the cause — this is the common case in interior layers. FLATTEN with %v (or return a fresh error) when you deliberately want to sever the chain — e.g. to stop leaking an internal cause across a public boundary, or to prevent callers coupling to an implementation error you may change. IGNORE only when the error is provably irrelevant (and say so with `_ =`). The failure modes: annotating everywhere without ever handling produces errors that climb to main() unhandled; handling (logging) at every layer double-logs and floods logs; flattening with %v when you meant to preserve the cause silently breaks errors.Is/As at the top; replacing a wrapped chain with a bare sentinel loses the debugging trail.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A per-call-site decision framework — handle vs annotate (%w) vs flatten (%v)/replace vs ignore — and the consequences of each at different layers.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go returns errors as values, so every call site must make an explicit choice; a coherent rule prevents the two dominant anti-patterns (double-logging and lost/leaked context) from creeping in across a large codebase.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Interior layers overwhelmingly annotate-and-return with %w (context accumulates, cause stays inspectable); exactly one boundary handles (classify, log once, map to a transport code, sanitize); %v/replacement is the deliberate exception used to cut the chain at a trust or API boundary.

theory.whyImportant: This is the operational core of 'handle once' — applying it consistently is what keeps logs clean, keeps the cause inspectable end-to-end, and stops internal details leaking across boundaries.
theory.realWorldExample: A repo annotates `fmt.Errorf("query users: %w", err)`; the service annotates `fmt.Errorf("list orders: %w", err)`; the HTTP handler handles once (errors.Is/As -> status, log the chain, generic client message); a public SDK method deliberately returns `fmt.Errorf("request failed: %v", internalErr)` to avoid leaking its internal cause type to third parties.

followUps.question: When is flattening with %v the RIGHT choice rather than a bug?
followUps.answer: When crossing a stable public API boundary where you don't want callers coupling to (or errors.Is-matching) an internal cause you reserve the right to change — you keep the human-readable context but intentionally drop the chain so the internal error type stays private.

followUps.question: Is it ever correct to both wrap AND handle at the same layer?
followUps.answer: Only at the single boundary: there you handle (log once, map to a status) — you don't also return it upward. Interior layers should wrap-and-return without logging; doing both at an interior layer is the classic double-logging bug.

scenario.question: Your microservice's logs are exploding in volume and on-call can't find the real cause of failures, yet clients sometimes see raw SQL errors in API responses. Diagnose and design a fix.
scenario.directAnswer: Two anti-patterns are at play: every layer is logging the same error (double/triple logging causes the volume explosion and obscures the real one), and errors are returned verbatim to clients (leaking internal details like SQL). Fix it with a layered strategy: lower layers ONLY wrap-and-return with %w (no logging); a single boundary (HTTP middleware/handler) logs the full chain once with structured fields, classifies the error with errors.Is/As, maps it to a status code, and returns a sanitized, generic message to the client. Internal causes never cross the boundary.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A handle-once, wrap-up, map-and-sanitize-at-the-boundary error strategy.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It separates the concerns of context-building (every layer) from outcome-deciding and logging (one layer), which controls both noise and information leakage.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Wrapping preserves a single rich error; the boundary is the only place that terminates it — log once, map once (errors.Is/As -> status), respond with a safe message.

scenario.whyImportant: Log noise blinds on-call during incidents, and leaking internal errors is a real security and trust problem.
scenario.realWorldExample: An API gateway middleware recovers/maps errors: not-found -> 404, validation -> 400, everything else -> 500 with body 'internal error' while the full wrapped chain and a trace ID go to the structured logger.

followUps.question: How do you correlate the client-visible error with the detailed log?
followUps.answer: Attach a request/trace ID: log it with the full chain and return it (or a short code) to the client so support can map a reported failure to its log entry.

followUps.question: Where do you attach structured fields like user_id or operation?
followUps.answer: Either via a custom error type carrying fields, or by logging them as separate structured fields at the boundary alongside the error — not by stuffing them into the error string.

scenario.question: After a refactor that moved sentinel definitions into a new shared package and 'cleaned up' some fmt.Errorf calls, several handlers that used errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) suddenly return 500 instead of 404 — but only sometimes. Diagnose the likely causes and how you'd fix and prevent it.
scenario.directAnswer: The intermittent nature points to broken chains, not a broken sentinel. Two refactor mistakes commonly cause this. First, a formatting verb was switched from %w to %v somewhere in the call path — %v flattens the sentinel into text and severs the chain, so errors.Is finds nothing below that point (it works only on paths that still use %w, hence 'sometimes'). Second, moving the sentinel to a new package can create a DUPLICATE definition: if some layer now constructs or compares against a different `errors.New("not found")` value than the one the handler imports, errors.Is (which matches by identity) fails because they're distinct values even with identical text. The fix: grep every layer on the failing paths for `%v`/`%s` wrapping an error and restore `%w`; ensure exactly one canonical sentinel is defined and imported everywhere (no re-declarations, no string comparison). Prevention: an errorlint/vet check that flags non-%w wrapping and == comparisons against error values, plus table-driven tests asserting errors.Is holds through the full wrapped chain (including deeply nested cases).

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A regression where wrapped-error identity is lost after a refactor, so boundary classification via errors.Is silently degrades to the default status.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: errors.Is depends on two invariants — the chain is preserved (only %w wraps) and the sentinel is a single shared value; refactors that swap %w for %v or duplicate the sentinel violate one invariant on some code paths but not others, producing intermittent misclassification.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: errors.Is walks the chain via Unwrap comparing each link to the target by identity (or a custom Is). A %v anywhere truncates the chain below it; a duplicate sentinel value never compares equal to the imported one, so the match fails even though the message text is identical.

scenario.whyImportant: Silent error-classification regressions cause real incidents (wrong status codes, missed retries) and are hard to catch because they compile and often pass happy-path tests — recognizing the %w/identity invariants is a senior-level diagnostic skill.
scenario.realWorldExample: A team split a monolith package and re-declared `ErrNotFound` in two places; repositories wrapped one, the handler imported the other, so errors.Is returned false and every miss became a 500 until they consolidated to a single sentinel and added an errorlint gate in CI.

followUps.question: How do you catch the %v-instead-of-%w mistake automatically?
followUps.answer: Enable go vet's errorf check and the errorlint linter — both flag `fmt.Errorf` that formats an error with %v/%s where %w was likely intended, and errorlint also flags == comparisons and type assertions against errors that should use errors.Is/As.

followUps.question: Why can two `errors.New("not found")` values with identical text fail errors.Is?
followUps.answer: errors.New returns a pointer to a distinct struct; errors.Is compares by identity (pointer equality), not text, so two separately-constructed sentinels are unequal — which is why a sentinel must be a single shared package-level var imported everywhere.

systemDesign.question: Design an end-to-end error-handling strategy for a large service exposed over both HTTP and gRPC: the error taxonomy, how domain errors map to transport codes, structured error responses, and observability. Where does mapping live and how do you keep it DRY across both transports?
systemDesign.directAnswer: I'd define a small, transport-agnostic error taxonomy in a shared package: a set of *kinds* — NotFound, InvalidArgument (validation), Conflict, Unauthorized, PermissionDenied, Unavailable (transient/retryable), Internal — expressed either as sentinels or, better, a typed `DomainError{ Kind Kind; Code string; Msg string; err error }` with Unwrap so it composes with %w. Domain and service layers wrap causes with %w and, at the point a condition becomes meaningful, tag them with a Kind. Mapping lives at the transport boundary in ONE function per axis: `kindOf(err) Kind` (uses errors.As to pull the DomainError, falling back to errors.Is on known sentinels, defaulting to Internal), then two thin adapters — `httpStatus(Kind) int` and `grpcCode(Kind) codes.Code` — so the classification logic is shared and only the final code table differs per transport. Structured response: a stable JSON body `{code, message, request_id}` for HTTP and status.Details for gRPC, carrying only the safe Code/Msg — never the internal chain. Observability: at the boundary log the FULL wrapped chain once with structured fields (kind, code, operation, user_id, trace_id) and increment `errors_total{kind=...}` so dashboards separate a 404 spike from a 500 spike; propagate trace_id to the client so support can correlate. Internal detail never crosses the boundary.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A layered strategy: a transport-neutral error taxonomy in the core, boundary interceptors/middleware that classify-map-log-sanitize once, and per-transport code tables.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Two transports over the same domain would otherwise duplicate mapping logic and drift; centralizing classification and sharing it keeps HTTP and gRPC behavior consistent and keeps internal causes off the wire.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Interior layers wrap with %w and tag a Kind via a typed DomainError. A single boundary component runs kindOf(err) once (errors.As for the typed error, errors.Is for sentinels, default Internal), then feeds the Kind to httpStatus or grpcCode, logs the full chain once with structured fields, emits a metric keyed by kind, and writes a sanitized response body carrying only Code/Msg/trace_id.

systemDesign.whyImportant: It's the archetypal 'errors at scale' design question: it forces you to separate classification (shared) from transport mapping (per-protocol), handle once, and guarantee no internal leakage — the exact discipline that keeps large services debuggable and safe.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: gRPC services use a boundary interceptor mapping domain errors to codes.NotFound/InvalidArgument/Unavailable while an HTTP gateway maps the same Kinds to 404/400/503; both call one shared kindOf(err) so the two code tables are the only transport-specific pieces, and both log the full chain once with a trace_id.

followUps.question: How do you keep retryable/transient classification consistent between transports?
followUps.answer: Model retryability as a taxonomy Kind (Unavailable) or an orthogonal marker checked with errors.As, decided once in the core; both httpStatus (503) and grpcCode (codes.Unavailable) derive from that single Kind, and internal retry layers check the same marker — one source of truth.

followUps.question: What stops internal error details from leaking to clients in this design?
followUps.answer: The boundary is the only place that renders a client response, and it copies only the taxonomy's safe Code/Msg plus a trace_id into the body/status — the wrapped chain (SQL text, internal IDs, stack info) is passed exclusively to the structured logger, never to the response writer.

coding.question: Implement a retryable-error mechanism. Define a way to mark an error retryable, and write `func IsRetryable(err error) bool` that returns true if any error in the wrapped chain is retryable.
coding.thoughtProcess: I want a property ('retryable') that survives wrapping. The clean way is a small wrapper type that carries the flag and implements Unwrap, plus a constructor Retryable(err). To answer the question through arbitrary wrapping, IsRetryable should use errors.As to find a *retryableError anywhere in the chain — that way fmt.Errorf("...: %w", ...) layers on top don't hide it.
coding.lineByLine: retryableError wraps an error and implements both Error (delegating to the inner message) and Unwrap (so errors.As/Is can see through it). Retryable is a constructor that tags an error, preserving nil. IsRetryable declares a target pointer and uses errors.As to search the entire chain for a *retryableError — so even after additional fmt.Errorf wrapping, the marker is still found.
coding.timeComplexity: O(d) where d is the chain depth (each Unwrap is O(1)).
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — no allocation beyond the single wrapper at tag time.

followUps.question: Why use errors.As instead of a type assertion?
followUps.answer: A direct type assertion only sees the outermost error; once wrapped by fmt.Errorf, the marker is buried. errors.As walks the chain and finds it regardless of depth.

followUps.question: How would a retry loop use this?
followUps.answer: After a failed call, `if !IsRetryable(err) { return err }`; otherwise back off and retry up to a limit, so only transient, tagged failures are retried.

coding.question: Implement a typed `DomainError` that carries a machine-readable kind and participates in the error chain (Unwrap), plus a boundary helper `HTTPStatus(err error) int` that maps any wrapped domain error to an HTTP status code using errors.As, defaulting to 500.
coding.thoughtProcess: I need an error that (a) carries a classification the boundary can branch on, and (b) survives wrapping so `fmt.Errorf("...: %w", domainErr)` layers don't hide it. So DomainError is a struct with a Kind enum, a safe message, and a wrapped cause; it implements Error() and Unwrap() (returning the cause) so it joins the chain. The boundary helper must find it no matter how deeply it's wrapped, so I use errors.As(err, &de) rather than a type assertion. The switch maps Kind -> status; the default (no DomainError found, or an unknown kind) is 500, which is the safe fallback for an unclassified internal error.
coding.lineByLine: Kind is an int enum giving a transport-agnostic classification with KindInternal as the zero value (safe default). DomainError holds the Kind, a client-safe Msg, and an unexported `err` cause; Error() renders message plus cause for logs, while Unwrap() returns the cause so errors.Is/As traverse into it. Wrap is the constructor that tags a cause and preserves nil. HTTPStatus is the boundary mapper: it declares `var de *DomainError` and uses errors.As so it locates the DomainError even under several fmt.Errorf(%w) layers; if none is found it returns 500 (the correct fallback for an unclassified internal error), otherwise it switches on Kind to the matching status, with the default arm also yielding 500.
coding.timeComplexity: O(d) where d is the wrapped-chain depth (errors.As does one Unwrap per link); the switch is O(1).
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — one DomainError allocation at Wrap time; HTTPStatus allocates nothing.

followUps.question: Why errors.As here instead of a type assertion `err.(*DomainError)`?
followUps.answer: A type assertion only inspects the outermost error; once the DomainError is wrapped by fmt.Errorf("...: %w", de) it's no longer the top of the chain, so the assertion fails. errors.As walks the chain via Unwrap and finds it at any depth.

followUps.question: How would you reuse this for gRPC without duplicating the classification?
followUps.answer: Keep kind extraction shared — factor out `kindOf(err) Kind` using the same errors.As — then write a second thin mapper `grpcCode(Kind) codes.Code`; both transports call kindOf so only the final Kind->code table differs, keeping classification DRY.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Adopt a layered contract: low-level layers wrap-and-return with %w and expose sentinels/typed errors as part of their public API; the transport boundary is the single place that classifies, maps to status codes, and logs. Define error families (NotFound, Conflict, Validation, Internal, Unavailable) in the package that owns each domain, and document which sentinels/types callers may match.
productionDeepDive.performance: Error handling is on the cold path, so wrapping cost is irrelevant; the real cost is logging. Centralize logging at the boundary to avoid N-times duplication. If you add stack traces (e.g. via a third-party error package), capture them once at origin, not at every wrap, since trace capture is comparatively expensive.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: When fanning out work, collect per-task errors and combine them with errors.Join (Go 1.20+) so callers can errors.Is/As across all of them. Guard shared error accumulators with a mutex or a channel; an errgroup.Group is the idiomatic way to wait and return the first error from a set of goroutines.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Classification drives reliability: mark transient failures (timeouts, 503s, connection resets) retryable so a retry/backoff layer can act, and mark terminal failures (validation, not-found) non-retryable so you fail fast. Reserve panic for truly unrecoverable states; recover at goroutine and request boundaries so one bad request can't crash the process.
productionDeepDive.observability: Log the full wrapped chain once at the boundary with structured fields (operation, resource, user_id, trace_id) rather than concatenating them into the message string. Emit metrics keyed by error class (e.g. errors_total{class="not_found"}) so dashboards distinguish a spike of 404s from a spike of 500s.
productionDeepDive.security: Never return internal error details (SQL text, file paths, stack traces, internal IDs) to clients — map to a generic message plus a trace ID at the boundary. Be careful that custom error types' Error() strings don't embed secrets, and that error-based logging doesn't capture PII without redaction.

caseStudies.problem: Callers need a stable way to detect 'no rows' without depending on a specific driver.
caseStudies.solution: Expose the sql.ErrNoRows sentinel; repositories translate it into a domain ErrNotFound with %w.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Sentinels are part of your public API and become hard to remove, but they give callers a precise, wrap-safe check via errors.Is.
caseStudies.lessons: Own your domain sentinels at the layer boundary; don't leak driver-specific errors upward.

caseStudies.problem: Map rich internal errors to a constrained set of wire status codes consistently.
caseStudies.solution: A boundary interceptor inspects errors with errors.Is/As and maps domain errors to codes.NotFound, codes.InvalidArgument, codes.Unavailable, etc., logging the full chain once.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Requires discipline to keep mapping centralized; the payoff is consistent client behavior and clean logs.
caseStudies.lessons: Map errors to transport codes in exactly one place, and keep the internal chain off the wire.

keyTakeaways: error is just the interface { Error() string }; wrap with fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err) to add context while keeping the cause inspectable — %w preserves the chain, %v drops it.
Inspect the chain, never ==: errors.Is matches a known sentinel anywhere in the chain, errors.As extracts a custom type so you can read its fields.
Handle each error once: lower layers wrap-and-return, a single boundary classifies, maps to a transport status, logs the full chain with structured fields, and returns a safe message.
Classify errors (retryable vs terminal, user vs internal), combine multiples with errors.Join, and reserve panic for truly unrecoverable faults — not ordinary control flow.
